title: West Asia War updates: U.S. in 'very deep talks with Iran', ready for military action if diplomacy fails, says Trump
summary: Fighting around the Strait of Hormuz paused after reciprocal halts by Iran and the U.S., but Tehran says it is not engaged in negotiations with Washington. President Trump said the U.S. is in "very deep talks with Iran" while warning of possible military action if diplomacy fails. Regional incidents — including drone interceptions, halted ship transits, Houthi strikes, and moves by Israel and Saudi Arabia — continue to disrupt shipping and push oil price volatility.
content:
Updated July 28, 2026 03:48 am IST

Iran’s Foreign Ministry said it was not currently involved in negotiations with the United States, despite a halt in recent fighting between the two sides. The ministry’s spokesman, Esmaeil Baqaei, denied reports that Iran had requested talks and said talks with Oman over the administration of the Strait of Hormuz "have no connection with the United States" and remain a bilateral matter.

The U.S. and Iran held their fire over the weekend, providing a temporary respite for Gulf shipping and the oil industry after weeks of missile strikes and air strikes. Tehran said it had halted retaliatory attacks against Washington’s allies in the region, and U.S. officials described President Donald Trump as giving diplomacy "a little bit of room" while forces remained "locked and loaded."

President Trump told reporters the U.S. was in "very deep talks with Iran" and warned he was prepared for "strong military action" if diplomacy failed. He also sought to reassure about munitions, saying U.S. ammunition stockpiles were ample even after five months of strikes. Trump said he would ask Russia’s Vladimir Putin if Russian satellites were assisting Iran’s strikes.

The conflict has spread across Gulf shipping lanes and nearby states. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy reported stopping multiple vessels trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz via routes not approved by Iranian authorities, firing warning shots and turning them back. State television said one vessel was involved in an "incident" though details were not elaborated.

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they targeted sensitive crude supply and transport sites linking eastern Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea city of Yanbu in response to alleged Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni airspace. Shipping through Bab el-Mandeb fell to its lowest level in months after Houthi attacks disrupted Red Sea traffic.

Regional militaries reported a string of interceptions and drone incidents. Saudi air defences said they destroyed drones launched from Iraq that targeted oil facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh, attributing the launches to Iran-backed groups in Iraq. Jordanian forces reported downing two drones with no casualties, and Israeli forces intercepted two UAVs near the Jordan border and were investigating their origin.

In Iran’s west, security forces said they killed four members of the outlawed Kurdish group PJAK following an armed clash, seizing weapons and ammunition. The incident was reported by state media and aligned with Tehran’s broader security operations near the Iraqi border.

The diplomatic and security developments influenced markets. Oil prices tumbled more than 5% on Monday after the U.S. and Iran paused strikes over the weekend, raising hopes of de-escalation and resumed shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude fell below a key support level intraday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate also declined sharply. The dollar weakened against major peers amid the shift in risk sentiment.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu departed for Washington to meet President Trump for talks focused primarily on Iran; it was reported as their first face-to-face meeting since the conflict escalated. The meeting underscored the close U.S.-Israel coordination amid the campaign against Iran.

Despite the lull, officials cautioned that the pause could be temporary. Fighting over the strategic Strait of Hormuz had derailed earlier diplomatic efforts and triggered an expanded U.S. air campaign and Iranian reprisals that affected shipping lanes, Gulf allies and military bases across the region. Observers warned that any resumption of strikes would quickly reverse market calm and further endanger commercial traffic.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry on Monday (July 27, 2026) said it was not currently involved in negotiations with the United States, despite a halt in recent fighting between the two sides.

Iran and the United States held their fire on Sunday (July 26, 2026), handing Gulf shipping and the oil industry a respite from missile strikes as Donald Trump’s UN envoy said the president was “giving talks some space”.

Iran said it had halted retaliatory attacks against Washington’s allies in the Middle East, and US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told Fox News Sunday that, while forces remained “locked and loaded”, Trump would give negotiations “a little bit of room”.

Prior to Friday (July 24, 2026), the U.S. military had carried out strikes on Iran for 13 consecutive nights, in the largest rekindling of the almost five-month-old war since an April ceasefire. Friday and Saturday nights passed without bombing.

Afrah al-Zouba, the Foreign Minister ‌Designate of Yemen’s internationally ⁠recognised Saudi-backed government said the Houthis ‌were seeking to replicate Iran’s ‌model ‌of ⁠trying to ⁠impose control on international shipping around the Strait ‌of Hormuz in the Bab el-Mandeb. The group had ‌been emboldened by what she called ⁠an insufficiently serious international response ‌to attacks on commercial shipping over the past years, al-Zouba ‌told a small group of journalists includingReuters

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday (July 27, 2026) dismissed concerns that ammunition stockpiles are running low after five months of bombing Iran, telling reporters: “We have a lot.”

Asked aboard Air Force One if he was concerned about munitions being depleted, Mr. Trump said: “We have a lot of ammunition. We have a lot of the mid-level stuff too, more than we could ever use no matter what.”

-AFP

U.S. President ‌Donald Trump said ⁠on Monday (July 27, 2026) he will ‌ask Russian ‌President ‌Vladimir ⁠Putin ⁠if Russian satellites are helping Tehran ‌direct strikes in West Asia.

“”i’ll ask Putin about ⁠it. We’ll find ‌out,” Mr. Trump told reporters aboard ‌Air Force One.

U.S. President Donald ‌Trump said on Monday (July 27, 2026) ⁠Washington was in “very deep ‌talks with ‌Iran” ‌and ⁠warned that he ⁠is ready for “strong military action” ‌if diplomacy failed.

“Not much time. Either ‌it goes fast or ⁠not at all,” ‌Trump told Axios when asked how long ‌he was willing to give ⁠for talks.

-Reuters

Iranian security forces killed four members of an outlawed Kurdish group in the west of the country near Iraq, state television said Monday (July 27, 2026).

“Following an armed clash between the brave border guards and these aggressor elements, four members of the PJAK group were killed,” police said in a statement carried by state TV.

Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) is proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Iran, Turkiye, and the United States.

“Significant amounts of weapons and ammunition, including several pistols, magazines, bullets, and hand grenades, were discovered,” in their vehicle near the city of Baneh in the western province of Kurdistan, the statement added.

-AFP

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ‌said that they ⁠targeted a number of ‌sensitive crude ‌oil ‌supply ⁠and transport sites ⁠linking eastern Saudi Arabia to ‌the Red Sea city of Yanbu.

The ‌group’s military spokesperson Yahya Saree ⁠said the action was ‌in response to what he described ‌as Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni ⁠airspace.

-Reuters

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu departed to Washington on Monday (July 27, 2026), where he said he would meet U.S. President Donald ‌Trump for their first face-to-face talks since the start of their conflict with Iran.

It will be Mr. ⁠Netanyahu’s eighth meeting with Mr. Trump since the U.S. President returned to office, and their first since February, right before Israel and the United States ‌launched a joint aerial campaign against Iran.

“In these complex times, you need to act with both great determination ‌and great wisdom. We will discuss all the ‌issues on ⁠the agenda, primarily Iran. Of course, our goal ⁠is to protect our security and also to expand the circle of peace around us,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a video statement upon departure.

Saudi Arabia’s ‌air defences intercepted and ⁠destroyed drones launched ‌from Iraq ‌that ‌attempted ⁠to ⁠target oil facilities in the kingdom’s ‌Eastern Province and Riyadh, ‌the Saudi Defence Ministry said ⁠on Monday (July 27, 2026).

The Ministry ‌said the drones were ‌launched by Iran-backed armed groups in ⁠Iraq.

-Reuters

Iran’s Foreign Ministry today said it was not currently involved in negotiations with the United States, despite a halt in recent fighting between the two sides.

“At present, we are not engaged in any negotiations with the United States,” said the Ministry’s spokesman, Esmaeil Baqaei, at a weekly press briefing, denying reports that Iran had requested talks.

Jordan’s ‌armed forces said ⁠they intercepted and ‌downed ‌two ‌drones ⁠on ⁠today morning, adding ‌that there were no casualties ‌or material damage.

The ⁠statement ‌did not identify ‌who launched the drones.

-Reuters

Iran’s Foreign Ministry today said the United States was not involved in recent talks with Oman over the administration of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

“These talks have no connection with the United States. They are a bilateral matter between Iran and Oman, and they are continuing,” said the Ministry’s spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, adding that the waterway “remains closed”.

-AFP

The Israeli military said it intercepted two drones today near the Jordanian border and was investigating where they had been launched from.

Earlier this month, the military said Israeli and Jordanian forces had intercepted an Iranian missile fired toward the Jordanian city of Aqaba.

“A short while ago, the IDF intercepted two UAVs identified in the area of the Jordan border,” the military said today.

-AFP

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy stopped six vessels attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through routes not approved by Iranian authorities, state television reported on today.

“Last night, six vessels that attempted to transit through a route other than the designated one were stopped by the IRGC Navy with warning shots and turned back,” a state television correspondent reported from the Gulf.

Earlier state TV said one vessel was involved in an “incident”, without elaborating.

On Saturday, the Guards said they had stopped four vessels attempting to transit through the southern part of the strait after firing warning shots.

-AFP

Iran and the United States held their fire today, handing Gulf shipping and the oil industry a respite from missile strikes as Donald Trump’s UN envoy said the president was “giving talks some space”.

Tehran said it had halted retaliatory attacks against Washington’s allies in West Asia, and U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz toldFox News Sundaythat, while forces remained “locked and loaded”, Mr. Trump would give negotiations “a little bit of room”.

Fighting over the strategic Strait of Hormuz derailed diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran, triggering a U.S. air campaign and Iranian reprisals that expanded the conflict to shipping lanes, Gulf allies and military bases across the region.

-AFP

Ship traffic through Bab el-Mandeb fell on Sunday after Yemeni Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the ⁠Red Sea coast, while transit through the Strait of Hormuz stayed low over the weekend, shipping data from Kpler showed on Monday.

Eleven commodity vessels passed through the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Sunday, ‌the lowest level in months, the data showed.

Red Sea traffic has been disrupted off the coast of Yemen since last week by the ‌Tehran-aligned Houthis, who want to blockade Saudi exports, expanding the U.S.-Iran conflict that has ‌already ⁠choked oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

-Reuters

Oil prices tumbled 5% on Monday ⁠after the U.S. and Iran paused strikes over the weekend after two weeks of attacks, raising hopes of a diplomatic solution that would de-escalate ‌the conflict and allow shipping to resume in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures fell $4.89, or 5.05%, ‌to $91.89 by 0009 GMT after briefly slipping under the ‌key ⁠support level of $90 earlier in the session.

U.S. West Texas ⁠Intermediate crude was at $84.64 a barrel, down $4.67, or 5.23%.

Both contracts are trading at their lowest levels in nearly a week after rising for the past three weeks.

- Reuters

The dollar slumped against its major peers at the start of Asian trading on Monday after the U.S. paused its ‌bombing campaign in Iran during the weekend, prompting a drop in oil prices and boosting ⁠global investor confidence.

Against the yen, the U.S. dollar was down 0.2% at 163.585 yen, its biggest decline since July 10. ‌The euro was up 0.2% at $1.1397, while the British pound rose by a similar magnitude to $1.3353.

Oil ‌prices sank in early Asian trade, with ‌Brent ⁠crude tumbling 4.7% to $92.19 after the U.S. military temporarily ⁠halted its two-week long strikes. Iran will halt its own attacks as long as the U.S. does the same, a senior Iranian official told Reuters ‌on Sunday, following a China-led push to resume stalled diplomatic efforts in Pakistan to end the war.

- Reuters
